Section 7 of such Act is hereby amended to read as follows:


“Sec. 8. 
There is hereby authorized to be appropriated annually to the Department of State, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, such sums as may be necessary for the payment by the United States of its share of the expenses of the United Nations as apportioned by the General Assembly in accordance with article 17 of the Charter, and for all necessary salaries and expenses of the representatives provided for in section 2 hereof, and of their appropriate staffs, including personal services in the District of Columbia and elsewhere, without regard to the civil-service laws and the Classification Act of 1923, as amended; travel expenses without regard to the Standardized Government Travel Regulations, as amended, the Travel Expense Act of 1949, and section 10 of the Act of March 3, 1933, as amended, and, under such rules and regulations as the Secretary of State may prescribe, travel expenses of families and transportation of effects of United States representatives and other personnel in going to and returning from their post of duty; allowances for living quarters, including heat, fuel, and light, as authorized by the Act approved June 26, 1930 (5 U. S. C. 118a); cost-of-living allowances for personnel stationed abroad under such rules and regulations as the Secretary of State may prescribe; communications services; stenographic reporting, translating, and other services, by contract; hire of passenger motor vehicles and other local transportation; rent of offices; printing and binding without regard to section 11 of the Act of March 1, 1919 (44 U. S. C. 111); allowances and expenses as provided in section 6 of the Act of July 30, 1946 (Public Law 565, Seventy-ninth Congress), and allowances and expenses equivalent to those provided in section 901 (3) of the Foreign Service Act of 1946 (Public Law 724, Seventy-ninth Congress); the lease or rental (for periods not exceeding ten years) of living quarters for the use of the representative of the United States to the United Nations referred to in paragraph (a) of section 2 hereof, the cost of installation and use of telephones in the same manner as telephone service is provided for use of the Foreign Service pursuant to the Act of August 23, 1912, as amended (31 U. S. C. 679), and the allotment of funds, similar to the allotment authorized by section 902 of the Foreign service Act of 1946, for unusual expenses incident to the operation and maintenance of such living quarters, to be accounted for in accordance with section 903 of said Act; and such other expenses as may be authorized by the Secretary of State; all without regard to section 3709 of the Revised Statutes, as amended (41 U. S. C. 5).”

fable.w: This section authorizes appropriations for the U.S. share of United Nations expenses and for salaries, travel and allowances of U.S. representatives and their staffs. The tempting reading is that the reference to rules and regulations the Secretary of State may prescribe amounts to rulemaking, but those rules only govern internal travel and cost-of-living allowances for federal personnel and involve no outside-party process. The General Assembly's apportionment of expenses is likewise not a consultation with outsiders before a federal decision. No comment period, hearing, advisory body, outside consultation or right to sue is created.
fable.s: under such rules and regulations as the Secretary of State may prescribe

qwen_block.w: This section is an appropriations provision that authorizes funding for the Department of State to pay its share of United Nations expenses and cover salaries and travel for U.S. representatives. It does not establish any process for consulting with or coordinating with non-federal entities (such as the public, states, or private organizations) before making a decision. The mention of 'representatives' refers to federal employees or appointees acting on behalf of the government, not outside participants in a decision-making process.
qwen_block.s: There is hereby authorized to be appropriated annually to the Department of State... such sums as may be necessary for the payment by the United States of its share of the expenses of the United Nations... and for all necessary salaries and expenses of the representatives provided for in section 2 hereof, and of their appropriate staffs

opus.w: The section gives the Secretary of State authority to prescribe rules and regulations, for family travel expenses and for cost-of-living allowances. Under the definition, and Example 6, granting an agency rulemaking authority counts as participation even when its use is optional. The tempting No reading treats the section as a pure appropriations provision. That reading has force because these rules govern internal personnel allowances, which are usually exempt from notice-and-comment, so this is a close call.
opus.s: cost-of-living allowances for personnel stationed abroad under such rules and regulations as the Secretary of State may prescribe
opus.b:
I labelled this Yes, but it's a close call. The section is mostly an appropriations provision, which on its own would not be participation. That would be the obvious reading.

1. **Why it might be No:** The section pays for the U.S. share of United Nations expenses and for staff salaries, travel and allowances. Paying for things is not participation. The "contract" mention covers buying services, which is also not participation. The rules mentioned only cover allowances for federal staff, so no outsider seems to be part of the decision.
2. **Why I chose Yes:** The section twice lets the Secretary of State issue "rules and regulations," for family travel expenses and for cost-of-living allowances. The definition counts rulemaking as participation, and Example 6 labels a statute Yes just because it lets an agency act "by regulation," even when that power is optional. Under that standard, these two grants of rulemaking power qualify.
3. **Why confidence is low:** These are internal rules about personnel pay, which are usually exempt from public notice-and-comment. If the outside-party test is applied strictly, the answer is No.

qwen_chat.w: This section is an appropriation provision authorizing funds for the Department of State to pay expenses related to the United Nations and for the salaries and expenses of U.S. representatives and their staffs. These representatives are federal officials or employees acting within the government structure. There is no requirement for consultation with outside entities, public comment periods, or advisory boards with non-federal members. The text describes internal government funding and operations.
qwen_chat.s: There is hereby authorized to be appropriated annually to the Department of State... such sums as may be necessary for the payment by the United States of its share of the expenses of the United Nations... and for all necessary salaries and expenses of the representatives provided for in section 2 hereof, and of their appropriate staffs
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "representatives... and their appropriate staffs" implies interaction with the public or other nations, but the text is purely an appropriation clause detailing funding for salaries, travel, and expenses of federal employees (U.S. representatives to the UN). It does not mandate consultation with outside parties, public hearings, or advisory boards involving non-federal members. The "representatives" are federal officials acting on behalf of the U.S. government.
